prompt.context: Our client is thinking about buying a piece of land in Jamaica for $3,000 and has asked us to determine whether or not this is a good idea.
prompt.question: Should our client purchase this piece of land in Jamaica? Is it a good investment?

clarifying_info.q: What is the purchase price of the land?
What is the client's financial target?
clarifying_info.a: $4,500 profit within the first two years, excluding the $3,000 purchase price

clarifying_info.q: What will the land be used for?
clarifying_info.a: Agriculture — the land can be used for real estate development, farming, holding and selling once it appreciates, etc. After candidate brainstorms, confirm the use will be agriculture.

clarifying_info.q: What crops or plants can be grown?
clarifying_info.a: Trees, Shrubs, Fruit, and Exotic Flowers

clarifying_info.q: Can you mix different plants on the same acre?
clarifying_info.a: No. Only one type of plant is allowed per acre.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price per plant?
What is the variable cost per plant?

clarifying_info.a: $500 initial setup (first year only), plus $350 per year for salaried labor

clarifying_info.q: What is the market demand per year?
Can the client capture the full market demand?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors cannot meet current demand. Competitor market shares: Trees 60%, Shrubs 20%, Fruit 85%, Exotic Flowers 90%. The client can capture the remaining share.

clarifying_info.q: How many plants fit on one acre?
clarifying_info.a: Trees 10/acre, Shrubs 25/acre, Fruit 75/acre, Exotic Flowers 50/acre (trees and shrubs take up more room)

exhibits.title: Case Sequence — Demand, Supply, Margins, and Profitability per Acre
exhibits.shows: A structured walkthrough of the analytical steps: computing client demand (market size × penetration rate), margins per unit (price minus variable cost), profitability per acre, and optimal acre allocation starting from most to least profitable crop
exhibits.data: Demand: Trees 2,000 units, Shrubs 800 units, Fruit 150 units, Exotic 250 units; Margin/unit: Tree $20, Shrub $10, Fruit $4, Exotic $8; Profit/acre: Tree $200, Shrub $250, Fruit $300, Exotic $400

framework: Clarify the objective: define what 'good idea' means (financial target = $4,500 profit in first two years, excluding $3,000 purchase)
Assess demand: determine market size per crop and client's achievable penetration rate given competitor shares
Determine supply constraints: 10 acres available, one crop type per acre, fixed plants-per-acre limits
Calculate unit economics: price minus variable cost to get margin per unit, then margin per unit × plants per acre to get profit per acre
Rank crops by profitability per acre and allocate acres from most to least profitable until demand is met
Calculate total two-year profit accounting for fixed costs ($500 setup in Year 1, $350 labor each year)
Compare total profit to $4,500 target and make a recommendation

questions.prompt: What is the client's estimated annual demand for each crop type?
questions.guidance: Multiply total market demand by the share competitors leave unmet. Trees: 5,000 × 40% = 2,000 units. Shrubs: 1,000 × 80% = 800 units. Fruit: 1,000 × 15% = 150 units. Exotic Flowers: 2,500 × 10% = 250 units.

math.setup: Client demand = Market demand × (1 − competitor share)

questions.prompt: What is the margin per unit and profit per acre for each crop?
questions.guidance: Margin per unit = price − variable cost. Profit per acre = margin per unit × plants per acre. Candidate should rank by profit per acre: Exotic ($400) > Fruit ($300) > Shrub ($250) > Tree ($200).

math.setup: Margin/unit = Price − Variable Cost; Profit/acre = Margin/unit × Plants per acre
math.answer: Profit per acre — Exotic $400 | Fruit $300 | Shrub $250 | Tree $200

questions.prompt: How should the 10 acres be allocated across crops to maximize profit, given demand constraints?
questions.guidance: Allocate acres starting from the most profitable crop (Exotic Flowers) until client demand is met, then move to the next. Trees are never needed because demand is satisfied before reaching them. All 10 acres should be assigned.

math.setup: Acres needed = Demanded units ÷ Plants per acre; allocate greedily from highest to lowest profit/acre
steps: Shrubs: 800 units ÷ 25/acre = 32 acres needed but only 3 acres remain — use 3 acres
Trees: demand satisfied or no acres left — 0 acres
math.answer: 5 acres Exotic Flowers, 2 acres Fruit, 3 acres Shrubs, 0 acres Trees

questions.prompt: What is the total profit over the first two years? Does it meet the $4,500 target?
questions.guidance: Calculate annual gross profit from each crop allocation, then subtract fixed costs for each year. Year 1 includes $500 setup cost. Year 2 does not. Sum the two years.

math.setup: Annual gross profit = sum of (acres × profit/acre) for each crop; Net profit = gross profit − fixed costs
math.answer: $5,500 total profit over two years, exceeding the $4,500 target by $1,000

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible uses for the Jamaican land? (Ask candidate to brainstorm before revealing agriculture.)

categories.name: Hold and Appreciate
ideas: Buy and hold for land appreciation
Sell once tourism drives up land values

recommendation: Recommend that the client purchase the Jamaican land

Under an optimal agricultural allocation (5 acres Exotic Flowers, 2 acres Fruit, 3 acres Shrubs), the investment generates $5,500 profit over the first two years, exceeding the $4,500 target by $1,000
risks: Demand growth or contraction for agricultural products could change the feasibility
Natural disasters — hurricanes, drought, and plant disease pose material risks in Jamaica
Competitor capacity expansion could erode the client's available market share
Foreign land ownership regulations or political/currency risk in Jamaica
next_steps: Investigate historical demand growth rates and market stability for each crop
Conduct due diligence on natural disaster risk and available insurance
Confirm legal ability to purchase and operate agricultural land as a foreign investor
Explore whether all-in on Exotic Flowers (if demand were available) would be optimal versus diversification benefits
